title: Polis
summary: The polis was an independent Greek political community combining government, law, religion, military defense, and civic identity.

title: Greek Geography
summary: Mountainous terrain encouraged political fragmentation and the development of many independent poleis.

title: Athens
summary: Athens politically integrated the communities of Attica into one polis.

title: Solon
summary: Solon addressed social conflict through reforms including debt relief and broader political participation tied to wealth.
key: reform of debt and political participation

title: Cleisthenes
summary: Cleisthenes reorganized Athenian citizens into new political units and helped broaden participation, earning a central place in the development of democracy.

title: Athenian Assembly
summary: Male citizens in the Athenian Assembly could debate and vote directly on public policy.

title: Athenian Courts
summary: Large citizen juries made legal judgment another major form of democratic participation in Athens.

title: Athenian Citizenship
summary: Athenian democracy excluded women, enslaved people, and resident foreigners from full political citizenship.

title: Historiography
summary: Herodotus used inquiry, travel, testimony, and comparison of accounts to investigate the past.

title: Greek Identity
summary: Shared language, religious festivals, myths, and customs helped create a Pan-Hellenic identity across separate poleis.

title: Greek Warfare
summary: The hoplite phalanx depended on disciplined cooperation because each soldier’s shield helped protect a neighbor.

title: Agora
summary: The agora served as a central public space for commerce, conversation, and civic activity in many Greek poleis.

title: Arete
summary: Arete meant excellence or fulfillment of valued qualities and could include courage, reason, skill, and service to the community.

title: Socrates
summary: Socrates used questioning to examine assumptions about justice, virtue, knowledge, and the good life.

title: Plato
summary: Plato imagined an ideal political order guided by wisdom and argued that rulers should possess philosophical knowledge.

title: Aristotle
summary: Aristotle studied actual political systems and emphasized observation and practical analysis.

title: Plato & Pythagoras
summary: Pythagorean ideas about number, proportion, and harmony influenced Plato’s view that reality had an intelligible order.

title: Hippocrates
summary: Hippocratic medicine emphasized natural causes, careful observation, and ethical medical practice.

title: Greek Medicine
summary: Greek physicians developed systematic diagnosis and prognosis based on observing symptoms and the course of disease.

title: Aristarchus
summary: Aristarchus proposed a heliocentric model in which Earth moved around the Sun.

title: Olympic Games
summary: The Olympic Games combined religious festival, athletic competition, arete, and Pan-Hellenic identity.

title: Greek Temple
summary: A temple sanctuary marked sacred space associated with the deity and worship.

title: Sparta
summary: The agoge trained Spartan boys in discipline, endurance, obedience, and military service.

title: Sparta
summary: Tradition associated Spartan iron currency with discouraging luxury, easy accumulation of wealth, and outside commerce.

title: Athenian Education
summary: Athenian education for elite boys included literacy, music, physical training, rhetoric, and preparation for civic life.

title: Cyrus the Great
summary: Cyrus defeated Median power and built the foundation of the Achaemenid Persian Empire.

title: Darius
summary: Darius governed a vast empire that required administration, taxation, roads, and control of repeated revolts.
key: challenges of governing a large empire

title: Ionian Revolt
summary: The Ionian Revolt helped trigger the Greco-Persian Wars by bringing Greek cities in Asia Minor into rebellion against Persian rule.

title: Battle of Marathon
summary: At Marathon in 490 BCE, Athenian-led forces defeated a Persian invasion, strengthening Athenian confidence.

title: Thermopylae
summary: The stand at Thermopylae demonstrated how terrain and disciplined resistance could delay a much larger Persian force.

title: Battle of Salamis
summary: The Greek naval victory at Salamis in 480 BCE damaged Persian naval power and helped turn the invasion.

title: Delian League
summary: The Delian League began as an alliance against Persia but increasingly became an instrument of Athenian power.

title: Athenian Golden Age
summary: Tribute and resources connected to the Delian League supported Athenian military power and monumental building.
key: resources supporting Athenian power and art

title: Peloponnesian War
summary: The Peloponnesian War pitted Athens and its allies against Sparta and its allies and weakened the Greek world.
key: inter-Greek war that weakened major poleis

title: Sicilian Expedition
summary: Athens’ Sicilian Expedition ended disastrously and destroyed major forces, weakening Athens during the Peloponnesian War.

title: Thrasybulus
summary: Thrasybulus helped overthrow the Thirty Tyrants and restore Athenian democracy after the Peloponnesian War.

title: Corinthian War
summary: Persian intervention in the Corinthian War illustrates how outside funding and diplomacy could shape conflicts among Greek states.

title: Leuctra
summary: Theban victory at Leuctra in 371 BCE broke Spartan military supremacy.

title: Philip II
summary: Philip II strengthened Macedonia and defeated a coalition of Greek states, preparing the way for Alexander.

title: Alexander the Great
summary: Alexander’s conquests spread Greek language and culture while also encouraging cultural blending across a vast empire.

title: Hellenistic Art
summary: Hellenistic art often emphasized movement, emotion, drama, age, and diverse subjects more strongly than earlier Classical idealism.

title: Long Walls
summary: Athens’ Long Walls connected the city to Piraeus, preserving access to naval power, trade, and imported food.

title: Early Rome
summary: Roman tradition dated the founding of Rome to 753 BCE and told stories of Romulus and Remus.

title: Etruscan Influence
summary: Early Rome borrowed religious symbols, engineering practices, political customs, and urban traditions from Etruscan neighbors.

title: Tullus Hostilius
summary: The traditional destruction of Alba Longa under Tullus Hostilius symbolizes Rome’s early aggressive regional expansion.

title: Roman Consuls
summary: The Republic used two annually elected consuls to divide executive authority and reduce the danger of monarchy.

title: Roman Senate
summary: The Senate became a powerful council dominated by elite families and influenced finance, diplomacy, and policy.

title: Patricians
summary: Patricians were associated with Rome’s old aristocratic families and early political privilege.

title: Plebeians
summary: The Struggle of the Orders describes plebeian efforts to gain political protections and greater access to office and law.
key: social conflict leading to political concessions

title: Tribunes
summary: Tribunes of the plebs could protect plebeians and use the veto against actions harmful to them.

title: Twelve Tables
summary: The Twelve Tables made key legal rules public and became an important symbol of written Roman law.

title: Cincinnatus
summary: Cincinnatus became a Roman model of civic virtue because tradition said he surrendered emergency power and returned to private life.

title: Salt and Early Rome
summary: Access to salt and trade routes helped make Rome’s location economically valuable.
key: trade and preservation value of salt

title: Roman Roads
summary: Road building linked communities, supported trade, administration, and military movement as Roman power expanded.

title: Punic Wars
summary: The Punic Wars were a series of conflicts between Rome and Carthage that transformed Rome into the dominant western Mediterranean power.

title: Hannibal
summary: Hannibal’s invasion of Italy across the Alps was an innovative attempt to defeat Rome on its own territory.

title: Cannae
summary: At Cannae, Hannibal used encirclement to destroy a much larger Roman army, demonstrating tactical flexibility.

title: Scipio Africanus
summary: Scipio shifted the war to North Africa and adapted tactics that helped defeat Hannibal at Zama.

title: Battle of Zama
summary: The Roman victory at Zama in 202 BCE ended the Second Punic War and broke Carthaginian military power.
key: Roman victory ending Second Punic War

title: Roman Conquest of Greece
summary: Rome increasingly intervened in Greek conflicts and eventually destroyed Corinth in 146 BCE, consolidating control.

title: Caesar and Pompeia
summary: The Bona Dea scandal produced Caesar’s famous claim that his wife had to be above suspicion, illustrating elite reputation politics.

title: Caesar and the Rubicon
summary: Caesar’s crossing of the Rubicon in 49 BCE symbolized the breakdown of Republican norms and the start of civil war.

title: Republic to Empire
summary: The late Republic’s civil wars and concentration of military loyalty contributed to a shift from shared republican rule toward one-man imperial power.

title: Augustus
summary: Augustus maintained republican titles and institutions while concentrating real authority in the principate.

title: Roman Roads
summary: Roads enabled rapid troop deployment, administration, communication, and movement of goods across Roman territory.

title: Roman Provinces
summary: Provincial government allowed Rome to administer conquered territories through governors, taxation, law, and military presence.

title: Pax Romana
summary: The Pax Romana describes a long period of relative imperial stability that encouraged trade, travel, urban growth, and cultural exchange.

title: Paterfamilias
summary: Roman family law traditionally placed major household authority in the male head of family, the paterfamilias.

title: Women and Guardianship
summary: Legal guardianship illustrates the restrictions placed on Roman women even when some elite women gained property or social influence.

title: Manus Marriage
summary: In manus marriage, a woman entered the legal authority of her husband or his family.

title: Political Marriage
summary: Elite Roman marriages could connect powerful families and function as tools of political strategy.

title: Roman Engagement
summary: Early engagement and marriage practices often reflected family strategy, inheritance, and social alliances more than individual romantic choice.

title: Agrippina the Elder
summary: Agrippina the Elder shows that elite Roman women could exert informal political or military influence without holding formal command.

title: Roman Slavery
summary: Enslaved people performed domestic, agricultural, industrial, educational, and administrative labor throughout Roman society.

title: Patronage
summary: Roman patron-client relationships exchanged protection, access, influence, and services across unequal social ranks.

title: Roman Baths
summary: Public baths functioned as places for hygiene, exercise, leisure, and social interaction.

title: Roman Busts
summary: Portrait busts helped preserve identity, ancestry, status, and memory in Roman visual culture.

title: Verism
summary: Veristic portraiture emphasized age, wrinkles, and distinctive features to communicate experience and civic seriousness.

title: Roman Concrete
summary: Opus caementicium gave Roman builders flexibility for vaults, domes, large structures, and durable marine construction.

title: Basilica
summary: The Roman basilica’s spacious hall and aisles made the form useful for later Christian congregational worship.

title: Column Base
summary: A column base transfers the shaft’s load into the supporting structure and can also contribute to the architectural order.

title: Roman State Religion
summary: Roman public religion emphasized correct ritual, sacrifice, priesthoods, and maintaining favorable relations with the gods.
key: ritual practice tied to civic life

title: Religious Syncretism
summary: Roman religion was highly adaptable and frequently identified, adopted, or blended deities and practices from conquered peoples.

title: Imperial Cult
summary: The imperial cult linked loyalty to emperor and empire with public ritual, civic identity, and political authority.

title: Stoicism
summary: Stoicism taught self-control, reason, duty, and living according to nature, making it attractive to many Roman elites and public servants.

title: Epicureanism
summary: Epicurean ethics sought tranquility and freedom from unnecessary fear and pain through moderation, friendship, and rational understanding.

title: Neoplatonism
summary: Neoplatonism developed a philosophical tradition centered on a highest principle and the soul’s ascent toward unity and truth.

title: Christianity in Rome
summary: Christianity grew from a minority movement into a major imperial religion, changing Roman religious and cultural life.

title: Religion and Authority
summary: Roman rulers and institutions used religious offices, rituals, omens, and sacred symbols to legitimize political authority.

title: Democratic Legacy
summary: Modern democratic participation draws on Greek examples of citizen debate and voting while expanding citizenship far beyond ancient limits.

title: Rule of Law
summary: Modern constitutional systems draw on Roman traditions of written law, legal procedure, citizenship, and interpretation while transforming them in new contexts.
key: Roman legal influence adapted to modern law

title: Classical Education Legacy
summary: Teaching logic, rhetoric, critical thinking, philosophy, and civic reasoning continues important Greek and Roman intellectual traditions.

title: Neoclassical Architecture
summary: Columns, pediments, symmetry, and monumental classical forms are often used by modern governments to signal stability, authority, rationality, and civic order.

title: Constitutional Courts
summary: Constitutional courts reflect ideals of stable written law, legal interpretation, precedent, and limits on political power.

title: Republican Legacy
summary: Modern representative government combines ideas of civic participation with institutional structures, divided offices, and legal limits on power.

title: Latin Legacy
summary: Latin influenced modern vocabulary, law, science, religion, and the development of Romance languages.

title: Infrastructure Legacy
summary: Roman roads, bridges, aqueducts, concrete, and urban planning remain models for how infrastructure can integrate large societies.

title: Artistic Legacy
summary: Greek idealism, Hellenistic expression, and Roman realism continue to influence later Western art and public monuments.

title: Citizenship Legacy
summary: Modern citizenship expands beyond the narrow categories of ancient Athens and Rome while retaining ideas of rights, duties, public participation, and law.
